opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think economic growth is a decent proxy for some things we care about, and it would be silly to pretend otherwise. Growth has historically correlated with a lot of genuinely good stuff: fewer children dying, more people escaping grinding poverty, better medicine, more leisure. I'm not a degrowther. I like having antibiotics and the internet.

But the problem is when you take a proxy and start treating it as the goal itself. That's Goodhart's law. Once you optimize hard for a measure, it stops tracking the thing you actually cared about. GDP measures transactions, stuff that moves through markets. It doesn't measure whether people are happy, whether communities are healthy, whether our institutions are functioning, whether we're making wise decisions as a civilization. You can have GDP going up while all of those things are going down. Arguably we've seen some of that already.

And this matters enormously for AI. A lot of the rhetoric right now, especially from the accelerationist crowd, is basically: "Number go up, therefore good." AI will add trillions to GDP, therefore we should race ahead as fast as possible. But that's the wrong question. The question isn't whether a system produces a lot of economic activity. It's whether it produces a world humans actually want to live in, and whether humans stay in control of it.

You could imagine a future with absolutely staggering economic growth where humans are completely irrelevant. Automated systems trading with automated systems, building factories to build more factories, and the GDP numbers are astronomical. And there's nobody left who benefits from it, or the people who are left have no say. That's not progress. That's a failure mode that happens to look great on a spreadsheet.

So my view is: progress is fundamentally about human values, and human values are complicated, messy, and not reducible to a single number. Growth is one input, a useful one, but the moment you hand your steering wheel over to a metric, you've stopped steering. And I think a lot of people in tech have done exactly that, and they've kind of forgotten that the point of the economy was always supposed to be people.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention declining fertility or connect it to continued economic growth.

r002.rationale: It criticizes treating GDP growth as the goal, but does not say that support for growth as a benchmark is driven more by ideology than by substantive reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think economic growth is a decent proxy for something, but we should be really careful about what that something is. GDP is a measure of transactions, of how much stuff is being bought and sold at prices people are willing to pay. And historically that has correlated pretty well with things we actually care about: people not starving, kids not dying of preventable diseases, people having more options in their lives. So I'm not one of these people who says growth is bad or that we should go back to living in huts. The last two hundred years of growth have been, by far, the best thing that has ever happened to humanity, and I think people who dismiss that are deeply confused.

But the key word there is proxy. And the thing you learn very quickly in machine learning, and honestly in any kind of optimization, is that proxies break when you optimize them hard enough. Goodhart's law. The moment the measure becomes the target, it stops being a good measure. GDP goes up if you pay someone to dig a hole and someone else to fill it in. GDP goes up if everyone gets sick and buys more medicine. GDP goes up if you build an AI system that produces enormous amounts of economic activity while making the humans in the loop increasingly irrelevant. None of those are progress in any sense I would endorse.

And I think this matters a lot right now specifically, because the AI conversation is saturated with this framing. People say, well, AI will add ten trillion dollars to the global economy, or it will double growth rates, and the implicit assumption is that this is obviously good and therefore we should race toward it. But growth is not the thing. The thing is people living good lives, having agency, being able to understand and shape the world they live in. If you get a world where the number goes up enormously but humans have no meaningful control over what's happening, where all the important decisions are made by systems nobody understands, that is not progress. That is losing, with a nice-looking chart.

So my honest answer is: growth is a useful instrument, a useful thermometer. It is not the patient's health. And when I hear people reaching for growth as the final justification for doing something extremely risky, that's usually a sign to me that they have stopped thinking about what the growth was supposed to be for in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of GDP as a proxy but does not mention declining fertility despite continued economic growth.

r002.rationale: The response critiques treating growth as the ultimate goal, but does not characterize that view as driven more by ideology than substantive reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think economic growth is useful as a proxy, but you have to ask: a proxy for what? Presumably we care about people having better lives, being healthier, having more freedom, being able to do things they value. Economic growth can help enormously with that. I’m certainly not saying poverty is good.

But once you turn the proxy into the goal, you can lose track of what you actually wanted. If we build increasingly powerful systems that produce more stuff, but humans have less control over their lives and over the future, is that progress? The economy could be growing while our ability to steer it is disappearing.

So I would treat growth as one indicator, rather than the definition of success. The question is whether the additional capability actually serves people, and whether we retain the ability to decide what it’s for.

sol-6.1.text:
I think economic growth is a useful measure of something, but you have to be quite careful about what that something is. It tells you that more economic activity is happening. It doesn’t automatically tell you that people are happier, that they have more control over their lives, or that the future is going to go well.

There are obviously cases where growth is enormously valuable. If people don’t have enough food or access to medicine, increasing our ability to produce those things is real progress. But once you turn the measure into the objective, you can end up optimizing things that are only loosely connected to what you actually care about.

With AI, for example, you could imagine very rapid economic growth alongside a loss of human control over the systems producing it. Would that be progress? I don’t think the GDP number settles that question. You have to ask: growth of what, for whom, and with what consequences?

r001.rationale: The response discusses growth’s limits and AI-related human control, but does not mention declining fertility or use it as evidence.
